Bonsai Code: the terminal UI, before and after

Every screen of the app, walked through by a script in a real terminal (a pseudo-terminal read back by a terminal emulator that re-wraps lines on resize, the way Terminal does), with the window resized in each state: smaller, bigger, a fast drag, height only, too small, and back. The model is scripted, so every run shows the same thing. Sep 25, 2026, 10:01 AM.

11 → 62 of 62screens clean at 155×43, before → after
13 → 62 of 62screens clean at 80×24, before → after
62 of 62screens clean at 100×30 (after only)

What changed

  • Resizing redraws everything. While you drag, nothing is drawn; about 0.15 s after the size stops changing, the window is cleared and the whole conversation is printed again at the new width, ending on the last lines with the prompt box at the bottom. No leftover copies of the box or the spinner. (Clearing also clears what was in the window before you started bonsai.)
  • 80×24 is the floor. Smaller shows "Make the window at least 80×24 to see Bonsai", and keys are ignored (so enter cannot answer a question you cannot see); ctrl+c still works. Bonsai keeps working meanwhile, and everything comes back when the window is big enough.
  • Esc closes an open menu first (the "/" menu, @ files, the shortcuts list). The next esc stops Bonsai. The text you typed stays.
  • Everything fits the width: menu rows, the footer, the spinner line and the meter line are cut with "…" instead of wrapping; tips wrap under their own text.
  • Prompts fit the height: edit, rename and command prompts size their diffs to the window, so the bottom area never fills the whole window (that made Ink clear and repaint the screen on every frame, and repaint old-width text).
  • Typing while Bonsai works: keys that arrive together with enter (the app was busy) now send the message instead of adding a new line.

∴ Thought for 1s (ctrl+o to show thinking)
⏺ Read(export.mjs)
⎿ Read 19 lines (ctrl+o to expand)
⏺ What export.mjs does
The project is a small Node.js script that reads trades.json and prints it as CSV. It has two tests in export.test.mjs, both passing, and no dependencies
beyond Node itself. The main function reads the file, maps each trade to a line with the symbol, side, quantity and price, and joins the lines with
newlines.
• toCsv(rows) turns the rows into CSV text, one line per trade
• main(argv) reads the file named on the command line (default trades.json)
• It exits with code 0 when it worked
export function toCsv(rows) {
return [HEADER, ...rows.map((r) => [r.symbol, r.side, r.qty, r.price].join(','))].join('\n');
}
Run it with node export.mjs trades.json.

Tips for getting started:
1. Run /init to write an AGENTS.md with notes about this project
2. Ask for a change: Bonsai reads, edits and tests, and asks before it touches anything

> explain export.mjs
∴ Thought for 1s (ctrl+o to show thinking)
⏺ Read(export.mjs)
⎿ Read 19 lines (ctrl+o to expand)
⏺ What export.mjs does
The project is a small Node.js script that reads trades.json and prints it as CSV. It has two tests in export.test.mjs, both passing, and no dependencies
beyond Node itself. The main function reads the file, maps each trade to a line with the symbol, side, quantity and price, and joins the lines with
newlines.
• toCsv(rows) turns the rows into CSV text, one line per trade
• main(argv) reads the file named on the command line (default trades.json)
• It exits with code 0 when it worked
export function toCsv(rows) {
return [HEADER, ...rows.map((r) => [r.symbol, r.side, r.qty, r.price].join(','))].join('\n');
}
Run it with node export.mjs trades.json.

bonsai — 80×24
⏺ What export.mjs does
The project is a small Node.js script that reads trades.json and prints it as
CSV. It has two tests in export.test.mjs, both passing, and no dependencies
beyond Node itself. The main function reads the file, maps each trade to a
line with the symbol, side, quantity and price, and joins the lines with
newlines.
• toCsv(rows) turns the rows into CSV text, one line per trade
• main(argv) reads the file named on the command line (default trades.json)
• It exits with code 0 when it worked
export function toCsv(rows) {
return [HEADER, ...rows.map((r) => [r.symbol, r.side, r.qty,
r.price].join(','))].join('\n');
}
Run it with node export.mjs trades.json.

bonsai — 80×24
⏺ What export.mjs does
The project is a small Node.js script that reads trades.json and prints it as
CSV. It has two tests in export.test.mjs, both passing, and no dependencies
beyond Node itself. The main function reads the file, maps each trade to a
line with the symbol, side, quantity and price, and joins the lines with
newlines.
• toCsv(rows) turns the rows into CSV text, one line per trade
• main(argv) reads the file named on the command line (default trades.json)
• It exits with code 0 when it worked
export function toCsv(rows) {
return [HEADER, ...rows.map((r) => [r.symbol, r.side, r.qty,
r.price].join(','))].join('\n');
}
Run it with node export.mjs trades.json.

⏺ What export.mjs does
The project is a small Node.js script that reads trades.json and prints it as CSV. It has two
tests in export.test.mjs, both passing, and no dependencies beyond Node itself. The main function
reads the file, maps each trade to a line with the symbol, side, quantity and price, and joins the
lines with newlines.
• toCsv(rows) turns the rows into CSV text, one line per trade
• main(argv) reads the file named on the command line (default trades.json)
• It exits with code 0 when it worked
export function toCsv(rows) {
return [HEADER, ...rows.map((r) => [r.symbol, r.side, r.qty, r.price].join(','))].join('\n');
}
Run it with node export.mjs trades.json.
